question: How can I make dashboard colors update automatically when metrics change?
answer:
In “Stop Being the Dashboard Color Police,” Isaac recommends conditional formatting. Set rules that link colors to metric values, such as red below target, yellow for a middle range, and green for strong performance. The dashboard will then update its colors automatically as the data changes.

Start with one key metric and test the traffic-light rule for a week. Keep the rules consistent, use no more than three or four main colors, and set thresholds that match business reality. You can later add gradients or more connected logic.

[chunk_id: stop-being-the-dashboard-color-police#6] Stop Being the Dashboard Color Police > Your Next Move
Don’t try to fix everything at once.

Start with one key metric. Add a traffic light rule; red, yellow, green. Let it run for a week. See what changes.

Then slowly add more rules, gradients, and connected logic. Make formatting part of your data story.

You’ll spend less time fixing visuals and more time finding insight.

Because the goal isn’t to eliminate your role. It’s to stop wasting brainpower on things a dashboard can do . So you can focus on what really matters.

---

[chunk_id: stop-being-the-dashboard-color-police#2] Stop Being the Dashboard Color Police > Real-Life Ways to Use It
Here are four practical formatting systems that work in real dashboards:

1. The Traffic Light System.

Use red, yellow, and green to show performance at a glance. Go further by using gradients ; light green for “barely made it,” dark green for “crushing it.”

2. The Heat Map.

Great for comparing lots of values across products, time periods, or regions. Let your eyes do the scanning. The hottest or coldest spots pop out instantly.

---

[chunk_id: stop-being-the-dashboard-color-police#1] Stop Being the Dashboard Color Police > What Is Conditional Formatting?
Conditional formatting is like giving your dashboard a brain.

It’s a simple set of rules that change the look of your data based on the values inside. If a number drops below target, it turns red. If it hits a new high, it glows green, all on its own.

Think of it as a traffic light system for your metrics. You set the rules once, and your visuals update automatically as the data changes.

It’s not just about making things colorful. It’s about creating visual cues your brain can understand instantly before you even read the number.

---

[chunk_id: stop-being-the-dashboard-color-police#4] Stop Being the Dashboard Color Police > ❌ Too Many Colors
A rainbow dashboard looks fun but tells no story. Stick to 3–4 consistent colors max.

❌ Only Red and Green.

Real data has nuance. Add yellow or use gradients to show shades of performance.

❌ Changing Color Rules Too Often.

If your red this month means what yellow meant last month, no one will trust the dashboard. Consistency is key.

❌ Arbitrary Thresholds.

Make sure your rules reflect business reality. If 85% is a win for your team, don’t make it look like a fail just because it’s under 90%.

question: How can I make my charts easier for people to read?
answer:
In “The Beginner’s Guide to Cleaner Data Visuals,” Isaac recommends simple changes that reduce noise and make the message easier to scan:

- Use text that is at least 12pt, with larger titles and headers.
- Left-align labels, legends, and text blocks.
- Start with a simple chart. Remove anything that does not add value.
- Make important data stand out with color and size. Keep axes and gridlines light.
- Use readable fonts, enough contrast, and colors that work for colorblind readers.
- Round numbers to sensible formats, such as 2.8M instead of 2,847,293.
- Add useful context, such as benchmarks, targets, or reference lines.

Isaac’s main point is to improve clarity, not remove every visual element. Keep anything that helps people understand the chart faster.

[chunk_id: the-beginners-guide-to-cleaner-data#0] The Beginner’s Guide to Cleaner Data Visuals > The Beginner’s Guide to Cleaner Data Visuals

That doesn't mean using bold colors or flashy designs. It means making smart, simple choices that help your message land. Small things, like font size or spacing, can do a lot of heavy lifting.

Okay, now you get to do the fun part. But even here, there's a right way and a wrong way.

Start simple. Don't add every bell and whistle your tool offers. Build the most basic version of your chart first, then add complexity only if it helps tell your story better.

Focus on the data, not the decorations. Your chart should highlight the important stuff and fade everything else into the background. That means:

- Make your data stand out with color and size

- Make your axes and gridlines light and subtle

- Only label the things that matter

- Remove any elements that don't add value

Make it readable. Use fonts big enough to read easily. Pick colors that work for colorblind folks. Make sure there's enough contrast.

[chunk_id: the-beginners-guide-to-cleaner-data#1] The Beginner’s Guide to Cleaner Data Visuals > 1. Make Your Font Bigger
This one's so simple it hurts. Yet we still squint at tiny text all the time.

Nobody likes playing detective just to read your axis labels. When you bump up your font size, people can actually focus on your insights instead of straining to see what you wrote.

If you think your font is big enough, make it bigger. Start with 12pt minimum for any text in your charts, and go even bigger for titles and headers. Your audience will thank you.

---

[chunk_id: the-chart-building-process-that-changed#5] The Chart Building Process That Changed How I Present Data > Step 5: Format Like a Pro
This is where good charts become great charts. The formatting is what makes people want to keep looking and actually understand what you're showing them.

Clean up your axes. Round your numbers to sensible values. If you're showing millions of dollars, don't display 2,847,293. Show 2.8M instead. Your audience will thank you.

Add context. A line that goes up is nice. A line that goes up 23% while the industry average went down 5% is a story. Add reference lines, benchmarks, or targets that help people understand if your numbers are good or bad.

Think about the “Signal-to-Noise” ratio. The Signal is the data and the clues that help you understand the numbers. The Noise is anything that distracts you.

A light gridline that helps you read a number is a signal.

An arrow pointing to a key insight is a signal.

If adding a little extra ink, like a border or a background color, helps your boss understand the chart in two seconds instead of ten, then do it.

[chunk_id: the-beginners-guide-to-cleaner-data#3] The Beginner’s Guide to Cleaner Data Visuals > 3. Left-Align Your Labels

question: What should I put at the top of my dashboard so people understand it quickly?
answer: Put your most important insight at the top left. Use the whole top row as a headline, with the key numbers and a short message that explains what happened. People should understand the current situation in five seconds or less. Keep details, long tables and extra notes lower down.
excerpts:
[chunk_id: your-dashboard-has-a-reading-order#2] Your Dashboard Has A Reading Order > Treating Your Dashboard Like A Story
You can fix this easily by changing how you lay things out. Every good story has a clear start, a middle, and an end. Your dashboard should work the exact same way.

The top left corner is your best spot. It is the very first place eyes land, so the whole top row should act like a giant headline. This is your beginning.

Put your most important numbers right here to tell people what happened in just five seconds. A simple message like “Sales are down 12% this month” is clear and impossible to miss.

The middle of your screen is where you back up your big headline. This is the perfect home for your main charts, trends, and comparisons. You are simply showing your audience why that top number looks the way it does.

It gives them the background they need to fully understand the story.

Finally, the bottom of the page is the end of your story. This is where the fine print goes. Save your long tables and extra notes for this area. People will gladly scroll down when they want to dig into those smaller details.

When you set up your page this way, everything feels completely natural, and your audience never has to guess where to look.

---

[chunk_id: your-dashboard-has-a-reading-order#0] Your Dashboard Has A Reading Order > Your Dashboard Has A Reading Order
Most people look at a screen the same way they read a book.

They start at the top left, move their eyes to the right, and then drop down a line. They do this over and over until they reach the bottom of the page.

It is just how our brains work.

This means the moment someone opens your dashboard, their eyes are already moving. They will treat whatever is in the top left as the most important thing.

The question is, did you put the right thing there?

---

[chunk_id: your-dashboard-has-a-reading-order#3] Your Dashboard Has A Reading Order > The Best Way To Help Your Audience
You might think you are just someone who works with data, but you are actually a designer. The way you place your charts changes how easily people understand your hard work.

Your dashboard already has a reading order, even if you did not plan it. What matters is if that order helps your audience or slows them down.

Start at the top left. Put your most important insight there. Build the rest of the story around it. And the next time someone says your dashboard is confusing, you’ll know exactly where to look first.

---

[chunk_id: the-best-dashboard-youll-ever-use#4] The Best Dashboard You’ll Ever Use Has Only 4 Metrics > How to Apply This to Your Dashboards
So how do you make your data dashboards more like car dashboards? Here are some practical steps:

Start with the core question. What's the one most important thing this dashboard needs to answer? That's your speedometer. Everything else is secondary.

Use the 5-second rule. Someone should be able to look at your dashboard and understand the current situation in five seconds or less. If they can't, you've got too much going on.

Group related information. Just like car dashboards group engine-related warnings together, group your related metrics. Don't scatter similar information all over the place.

Make status clear. Use colors, icons, and visual cues to show whether things are good, bad, or need attention.

Hide the details. Not everything needs to be visible all the time. Let people drill down into details when they need them, but keep the main view clean.

The hardest part of building better dashboards isn’t technical. It’s mental.

It’s the ability to not show everything. To trust that clarity beats completeness. To design with purpose, not panic.

Remember, the goal isn't to show off how much data you can collect.

The goal is to help people make better decisions, faster.

---

[chunk_id: steai-the-layout-before-you-build#3] SteaI the layout before you build the dashboard > Step 3: Sketch Before You Click
This step separates the pros from the amateurs, and it takes maybe 10 minutes.

Grab whatever's handy – a notebook, the back of an envelope, PowerPoint, even a napkin. Draw boxes where things should go:

- Big box at the top for your key metrics (your KPIs that everyone cares about most)

- Medium boxes for your main charts

- Small boxes for filters and controls

- Don't forget space between everything

Think of it like planning where furniture goes in a room before you start moving heavy stuff around.

- What's the most important thing? Put it where people look first (top left, then top center)

- What goes together? Group related charts near each other

- How will people use this? Put filters where they're easy to find but not in the way

question: How do I choose the right bar chart for comparing totals, parts, or percentages?
answer:
Start with what the reader should compare. Use a grouped bar chart when the goal is to compare categories or parts closely. Use a regular stacked bar chart when the total matters and the parts explain that total. Use a 100% stacked bar chart when the total size is not the focus and you want to compare percentage shares or mix.

Watch the trade-offs. Stacked bars make middle sections harder to compare. A 100% stacked chart hides actual totals because every bar has the same length. A grouped chart can make readers focus on small bars and miss the total. The chart should follow the message.
excerpts:
[chunk_id: the-bar-chart-mistake-most-analysts#1] The Bar Chart Mistake Most Analysts Make > What A Bar Chart Is Actually Supposed To Do
A bar chart is not just there to show numbers. Its real job is to help people compare things.

That sounds simple, but it changes how you think about chart choice.

Before you pick a chart, you need to ask one simple question: what should the reader compare?

Should they compare one category against another? Should they compare how smaller parts add up to a total? Should they compare the percentage share of each part?

Those are different questions. And each one needs a different type of bar chart.

---

[chunk_id: the-bar-chart-mistake-most-analysts#3] The Bar Chart Mistake Most Analysts Make > Stacked Bar Charts Show The Total And The Parts
A stacked bar chart is better when the total matters.

Instead of placing bars side by side, a stacked bar chart places smaller bars on top of each other. Together, those smaller pieces form one full bar.

This makes the chart useful when you want people to see the total amount and also understand what made up that total.

For example, let’s say you are showing monthly sales, split by product type. A stacked bar chart can help the reader see total sales for each month. At the same time, the colors inside each bar show how each product type added to the total.

That is useful when the story is about both the big picture and the parts inside it.

But stacked bar charts have a weakness. They are not great when you want people to compare each piece closely.

The first part of the bar is usually easy to compare because it starts on a flat line. But the blocks in the middle or at the top do not start from the same place. This makes them harder to compare with the eye.

So if you want the reader to compare Product B across five months, a stacked bar chart may not be the best choice. Product B may sit in the middle of each bar, and each piece may start from a different point. The reader now has to work harder to compare them.

That does not mean stacked bars are bad. Use them when the total matters and the parts are there to support the story. Do not use them when the main goal is exact comparison between each part.

---

[chunk_id: the-bar-chart-mistake-most-analysts#5] The Bar Chart Mistake Most Analysts Make > Choosing Well Is A Communication Skill
Picking the right chart is not just about knowing the tool. It is about helping people understand.

It means you are thinking about the person who will read the chart. It means you are asking what they need to understand first. It means you are choosing what is clear over what you always do.

If you use a 100% stacked bar chart when totals matter, the reader may miss that one group is much larger than another.

If you use a stacked bar chart when people need to compare each part, the reader may struggle with the middle sections.

If you use a grouped bar chart when the total matters, the reader may focus too much on each small bar and miss the bigger picture.

The data does not change when you switch from one chart type to another. But the story can change a lot.

That is why analysts need to slow down before building the chart.

Start with the question.

Then choose the chart.

The chart should follow the message, not the other way around.

---

[chunk_id: the-bar-chart-mistake-most-analysts#4] The Bar Chart Mistake Most Analysts Make > 100% Stacked Bar Charts Show Share
A 100% stacked bar chart looks like a regular stacked bar chart, but it does something very different.

In a normal stacked bar chart, the full height of the bar shows the actual total. A bigger bar means a bigger total.

In a 100% stacked bar chart, every bar has the same full length. Each bar represents 100%. The pieces inside the bar show the share of that total.

This chart is useful when the total size is not the main point. The focus is the mix.

For example, let’s say you are comparing traffic sources for three websites. One website may have 10,000 visits. Another may have 100,000 visits. But maybe your goal is not to compare total visits. Maybe your goal is to compare where the traffic came from.

In that case, a 100% stacked bar chart can help. It can show what share came from search, social, email, or paid ads.

This chart helps answer questions like: Which website depends more on search? Which one gets a higher share from email? How does the traffic mix change across websites?

That is where 100% stacked bars are useful. They help people compare shares.

But they also come with a risk.

Because every bar is the same length, the chart can hide the actual total. A small group and a large group can look equal, even when they are not.

That can be dangerous when the total size matters.

For example, 50% of 100 customers is not the same as 50% of 10,000 customers. The percentage is the same, but the meaning is very different.

So use 100% stacked bar charts when the share is the main message. Avoid them when the actual total is important to the decision.

question: How can I add context so people understand unusual changes in my charts?
answer:
Add short annotations directly to the chart when there is a spike, dip, strange pattern, or important takeaway. Say what happened and, when you know it, why. For example, label a jump “2013: New policy introduced” or a dip “Holiday spike” or “School break dip.”

You can also add reference lines, benchmarks, or targets so people can judge whether a change is good or bad. For recurring patterns, compare the current period with last month and the same month last year, and note what is normal for that season before explaining what is different.
excerpts:
[chunk_id: your-chart-cant-explain-itself-but#4] Your Chart Can't Explain Itself (But It Should) > When Should You Use Them?
You don’t need to write a novel on every slide. That would be messy. But you should use annotations for the big moments:

- Spikes and Dips: Did the numbers jump or crash? Explain what happened (e.g., “Server outage” or “Holiday Sale”).

- Goals: If you are trying to hit a target, draw a line and label it “Goal.”

- Key Takeaways: If there is one thing you want people to remember, write it right on the chart.

- Weird patterns: If something strange shows up in the data, explain it.

---

We like to think a clean chart can explain itself. We think good colors and a clear title are enough.

But usually, context is everything.

A line going up looks like success, until you realize it’s counting customer complaints. A sudden drop looks like failure, unless you know a system outage caused it.

When you’re not there, people usually do one of three things::

- They guess the story (and get it wrong).

- They waste time hunting for answers.

- They ignore the data completely.

You need to leave your voice behind when you’re not there.

[chunk_id: the-chart-building-process-that-changed#5] The Chart Building Process That Changed How I Present Data > Step 5: Format Like a Pro
This is where good charts become great charts. The formatting is what makes people want to keep looking and actually understand what you're showing them.

Clean up your axes. Round your numbers to sensible values. If you're showing millions of dollars, don't display 2,847,293. Show 2.8M instead. Your audience will thank you.

Add context. A line that goes up is nice. A line that goes up 23% while the industry average went down 5% is a story. Add reference lines, benchmarks, or targets that help people understand if your numbers are good or bad.

Use color with purpose. Don't make everything rainbow colored just because you can. Use color to highlight what's important. Make the good stuff green and the bad stuff red only if that makes sense. Sometimes gray is your best friend.

---

[chunk_id: your-chart-cant-explain-itself-but#2] Your Chart Can't Explain Itself (But It Should) > Here’s What I Mean by Annotations
An annotation is just text you add directly to your chart to explain what is happening.

It isn’t fancy. It is literally you writing on the chart to make sure people understand what they are seeing. It works like a small road sign. It tells the reader: “Look here. This is important. Here is why.”

Let’s look at how this works in real life.

What Happened vs Why It Happened.

Take a look at the image below.

On the left, you see a line chart. It shows the number of studies funded. The line goes up and down, and then shoots way up in 2013.

The chart tells you what happened (numbers went up). But it doesn’t tell you why .

Now look at the right side. Same data. Same chart. But this time, there is a simple note: “2013: New policy introduced.”

Boom. Now you get it. You don’t have to guess. The policy change lines up with the jump. That little bit of text turned a boring graph into a clear story.

---

[chunk_id: the-line-doesnt-always-go-up#4] The Line Doesn't Always Go Up > 4. Talk to People Who Know the History
People who have been in the company for years know the rhythm.

You will hear things like:

- “Q3 is always slow.”

- “Engagement drops after big launches.”

- “Sales fall during school exams.”

Mix human memory with your data. It gives you strong context. These insights save you hours of digging through data.

How to Use This in Your Actual Work.

Once you spot a seasonal pattern, use it to guide your work.

Build simple baselines. Look at two to three years of data and note when dips and peaks usually happen. Add key factors like holidays or weather. Even one simple note like ‘Sales fall in Q3 and rise again in Q4’ helps a lot.

Add context to your dashboards. Never show one number alone. Include last month and the same month last year. A month to month dip looks scary until you see year to year growth.

Annotate your charts. Add small notes like “Holiday spike” or “School break dip.” This helps everyone understand the pattern without guessing.

Lead with context. When you present results, start by saying what is normal for that season. Then explain what is new or different. This keeps the focus on insight, not panic.

question: How can I explain the same metric differently to different teams?
answer: Isaac suggests keeping the metric fixed but changing the story to fit the team and its decision. Start with what that team cares about. For product, UX, or support teams, frame conversion as a user experience issue: 5 out of 100 visitors buy, while 95 leave. Then focus on where users struggle, such as the sign-up flow or unclear value, rather than treating the number as only a score.
excerpts:
[chunk_id: the-gift-and-risk-of-data-storytelling#0] The Gift and Risk of Data Storytelling > The Gift and Risk of Data Storytelling
You look at a dashboard and see this:

Conversion rate this month: 5.0 percent Conversion rate last month: 4.5 percent

Nice. It went up.

But what does that really mean?

- A marketer might say, “The new campaign is working.”

- A product manager might say, “Users are finding the value faster.”

- A finance lead might say, “Revenue is growing.”

- A support lead might say, “Tickets will go up again.”

All of them are reacting to the same metric.

This is why one metric can feel powerful and confusing at the same time. The number is fixed. The story around it is not.

The good news is that you can use this on purpose. You can shape the story to fit the audience and the decision.

To show this, let us walk through three stories for the same conversion rate.

---

[chunk_id: the-gift-and-risk-of-data-storytelling#2] The Gift and Risk of Data Storytelling > Story 1: The user story
This story looks at the people behind the metric. It cares about what they see, where they get stuck, and how the product feels.

You might say:

“Out of every 100 visitors, 5 end up paying for our product. So 95 people come, look around, and leave without buying. Our job is to understand why those 95 drop off.”

The metric now becomes a signal of user experience, not just a score.

The same metric supports a story like this:

“Our conversion rate is 5 percent, but it is not only a win. It is also a mirror that shows how many visitors we fail to help. If we fix the sign up flow and make our value clearer in the first 30 seconds, we can raise this number by making the experience better, not just by shouting louder in ads.”

Use this story when you talk with UX designers, product managers, and customer support. They care about friction and want to know where users are struggling.

judge_reason: Both checks pass: the answer addresses tailoring the metric’s story and stays within the excerpts.

question: How can I spot people missing from my survey data?
answer: In “The Data You're Not Looking At,” Isaac says to compare the number of responses with the number of people who received the survey. The gap shows how many people are missing. Then check whether missing responses cluster by age, region or another group. Those patterns may reveal that your survey method is missing certain people. Also study where people drop off and ask why people opted out. Don’t treat missing responses as random or ignore them. They may point to frustration, poor access or a problem with how the survey reaches people.
excerpts:
[chunk_id: the-data-youre-not-looking-at#3] The Data You're Not Looking At > How To See What Everyone Else Misses
You don’t need fancy tools to fix this. You just need to change how you look at the screen.

Every time you analyze data, ask yourself one simple question: Who or what is NOT in this dataset?

Here are some ways to find the answer.

- Compare your data to the whole group. If you have 500 survey responses, check how many people you sent the survey to. The gap between those two numbers is important.

- Look at your funnel. Don’t just celebrate the people who converted. Study the people who dropped off at each step. Where did they leave? Why did they leave?

- Check for patterns in who’s missing. Are certain types of people not showing up in your data? Maybe younger users aren’t responding. Maybe people from certain regions aren’t buying. That’s a clue.

- Ask why people opted out. If someone unsubscribed from your emails or left your platform, find out why. The people who leave often know more than the people who stay.

Beyond The Chart.

Anyone can make a chart based on the numbers in front of them. That is the easy part.

But the best analysts are the ones who notice what is missing. They look at the empty rows and realize something is wrong.

Don’t just count the hands that are raised. Ask why the other hands are down.

---

[chunk_id: the-data-youre-not-looking-at#1] The Data You're Not Looking At > We Do This Too
We do the same thing with data. We look at the survey responses we got. But we forget about the people who never answered.

We study the customers who bought our product. But we ignore the ones who looked and walked away.

We analyze the employees who stayed at the company. But we don’t ask the ones who left why they quit.

We’re looking at the planes that came back. We’re missing the ones that crashed.

---

[chunk_id: the-data-youre-not-looking-at#2] The Data You're Not Looking At > Listen to What's Not There
Let me show you what I mean.

Your team sends out a survey. You get 1,000 responses. You analyze them and find out that 90% of people are happy with your product. Amazing, right?

Wait.

How many people got the survey? 10,000.

That means 9,000 people didn’t even bother to reply.

Those 9,000 silent people might be so frustrated they did not want to reply. They might already be looking for a different product. They might be your real problem.

But if you only look at the 1,000 responses, you’ll never know.

The empty rows are trying to tell you something. You just have to listen.

---

[chunk_id: the-dirty-secret-every-senior-analyst#0] The Dirty Secret Every Senior Analyst Knows (But Won't Tell You) > The Dirty Secret Every Senior Analyst Knows (But Won't Tell You)
Data doesn't just appear. Humans create it.

And humans are weird, lazy, creative, and unpredictable.

That means every dataset you open is a mirror.

Not just of business processes, but of human behavior, pressure, habits, and workarounds. Clean it too fast, and you risk scrubbing away the most important clues.

This is the side of data work nobody talks about in tutorials.

The part that feels more like psychology than Python.

Let’s get into it.

In a sales dataset, if all the missing commission amounts belong to one manager, that's not a data quality issue. That's either a problem with their reporting system or they're hiding something.

If survey responses are missing for specific age groups, that's not random. That's telling you something about how those people interact with your survey method.

If timestamps cluster around certain hours, that's revealing when people actually use your product vs. when you think they do.

The pattern in what's NOT there is just as important as what IS there.

That person who bought 847 units of your product. Don't remove them. Find them. They might be running a business you didn't know existed.

Those users with session times of 14 hours. They're not errors. They're power users who left your app open, which tells you something important about your product's stickiness.

question: When should I show a percentage versus the actual numbers?
answer:
Use percentages when you need to compare things of different sizes, show growth rates, or explain a share relative to a whole. They make counts easier to compare and add context, such as showing whether 200 cancellations are serious for a company’s customer base.

Show the actual numbers when the starting base is small. Percentages can make a change from 2 sign-ups to 6 look like a major breakthrough, even though the result is still small. In practice, use both when possible: the percentage shows the rate of change, while the actual numbers keep the scale clear.

[chunk_id: a-million-dollars-at-a-startup-vs#4] A Million Dollars at a Startup vs. Amazon > So When Should You Use Each?
Here’s the simple rule I follow:

Use Percentages When:.

- You’re comparing things of different sizes. Percentages let you compare apples to oranges (or businesses of different scales).

- You want to show growth rates. If you’re tracking performance over time, percentages show the speed of change.

- Your base number is large enough to matter. If you’re starting with at least 100-1,000 data points (depending on context), percentages start making sense.

- You want to normalize data. Percentages help you say “this is how big this is relative to the whole.”

---

[chunk_id: average-and-sum-make-all-the-money#4] Average And Sum Make All The Money > Percentages Make Numbers Fair To Compare
Percentages help people compare things clearly.

If 50 people bought from 100 visitors, that is a 50% conversion rate. If 500 people bought from 10,000 visitors, that is a 5% conversion rate.

The second group has more buyers, but the first group performs better.

Without percentages, people may chase the bigger number and miss the better result.

Percentages help answer business questions like these:

What share of users became customers? What percent of sales came from this product? What percent of customers canceled?

Percentages turn plain counts into meaning. They help teams compare large groups and small groups. They also help people understand risk.

For example, 200 canceled customers may sound bad. But if the company has 200,000 customers, that may not be a crisis. If it has 500 customers, that is a serious problem.

The same number can mean different things depending on what you compare it to. Percentages make that clear.

---

[chunk_id: a-million-dollars-at-a-startup-vs#2] A Million Dollars at a Startup vs. Amazon > When Percentages Make You Look Silly
Percentages are great for showing relative change . They help you understand growth or decline in relation to where you started.

But here’s the catch: percentages amplify small numbers and hide context from big ones.

Example: The Misleading Small Base.

Let’s say you’re running a new marketing campaign.

- Week 1: You got 2 sign-ups

- Week 2: You got 6 sign-ups

You could say: “We increased sign-ups by 200%!”

Technically true. But also... meaningless. You went from 2 people to 6 people. That’s not really a breakthrough.

When your starting number is tiny, percentages make everything look like a miracle. But in reality, you haven’t proven anything yet.

Don’t use percentages when your base number is small. You’ll look like you’re trying too hard to impress people, and anyone who knows data will see right through it.

question: How should I arrange the information in my chart so people understand it quickly?
answer:
Arrange information based on what you want people to understand. For performance or comparison, order values from highest to lowest. For change or trends, use time order. For a natural sequence, use logical order.

Put the most important insight at the top left, and build the rest of the chart or dashboard around it. Write the title as a headline that states the main finding, then use the chart to support it.

Keep the design simple. Highlight key data with color and size, make axes and gridlines subtle, label only what matters, and remove anything that adds no value.

question: How do I choose the right dashboard for the people who will use it?
answer:
Choose the dashboard by the users’ role and what they need to do. Start with the one most important question it must answer, then show only the metrics that help answer it. Give different roles different views, rather than showing everyone everything.

Keep the main view simple enough to understand in five seconds. Hide extra detail behind drill-downs. If users need to explore data themselves, a dashboard fits. If they need one clear message, slides may work better.

Finally, watch real users. Their behavior will show whether the dashboard is useful, including which filters they actually use.

question: What skills should I build to stay valuable as AI handles more analyst tasks?
answer: Isaac argues that you should build skills around judgment, business knowledge, storytelling and trust, not just technical execution. Learn AI tools, but also understand how your company makes money, how its data is created, and what context sits behind the numbers. Practice explaining complex ideas to non-analysts, answering hard questions and helping people act. You should also learn to check data, explain what went wrong, and say what still needs caution. question: How can I make my analysis meaningful and recommend what people should do next?
answer:
Make the analysis serve a clear decision. Start with a specific problem or goal, explain the data and its limits, then show only the analysis steps that changed your direction. Keep findings tied to what the numbers support.

To make it meaningful, test each result with “So what?” If it does not connect to a business goal or change what the business should do, leave it out. Tailor the detail to your audience: executives need impact and actions, while analysts may need more method and detail.

End with a clear recommendation. Do not only describe a problem. Say what action to take, such as changing pricing, launching a campaign, focusing on a customer group or fixing a process. For dashboards, connect different scenarios to recommended actions, tools or workflows so the path from insight to action is short.

question: How can I tell whether a sudden drop is normal or something I need to fix?
answer:
Start by checking the historical data. Look at previous years and ask whether the drop happens at the same time, is a similar size, and usually recovers in the same way. If it repeats, it is probably seasonal.

Then check outside causes, such as holidays, weather, industry cycles or major events. Compare your results with industry benchmarks, competitors and the wider market. If everyone drops together, it is likely normal. If only your results fall while others grow, that is a red flag.

Also ask experienced colleagues about the usual rhythm. Isaac recommends using baselines, year-over-year comparisons and chart notes so normal seasonal changes are clear.

[chunk_id: the-line-doesnt-always-go-up#2] The Line Doesn't Always Go Up > Is It a Failure or a Season?
Here is a practical way to figure out what type of dip you are looking at.

1. Look at Your Historical Data.

Start with the past. Pull data from previous years and see if the dip appears again.

Ask:

- Does it happen around the same time each year?

- Is the size of the dip similar?

- How long did it take to bounce back before?

If the pattern repeats, you are looking at a season, not a failure.

---

[chunk_id: the-line-doesnt-always-go-up#3] The Line Doesn't Always Go Up > 2. Check External Factors
Some dips line up with events outside the dashboard.

Think about:

- Holidays and school schedules

- Weather changes

- Industry cycles

- Cultural moments and big events

If ad clicks crash during the Super Bowl, that is not a failing ad. People are simply watching TV.

3. Compare Against Industry Benchmarks.

Do not look at your data alone.

Check:

- Industry benchmarks

- Competitor trends

- Market movement

If everyone dips at the same time, it is likely seasonal. If only you dip while others grow, that is a red flag.

---

[chunk_id: the-line-doesnt-always-go-up#5] The Line Doesn't Always Go Up > Let’s Zoom Out for a Second
Data is not just numbers. It reflects human behavior. And human behavior moves in cycles.

People travel. People rest. People follow calendars, weather, and moods.

Not every dip needs a fix. Not every slowdown is a crisis. Many dips are simply seasons.

And when you learn to read those seasons, the data becomes easier to explain and easier to trust.

Your job is not to make every month go up. Your job is to know what is normal, spot what is different, and help people understand why.

---

[chunk_id: the-line-doesnt-always-go-up#4] The Line Doesn't Always Go Up > 4. Talk to People Who Know the History
People who have been in the company for years know the rhythm.

You will hear things like:

- “Q3 is always slow.”

- “Engagement drops after big launches.”

- “Sales fall during school exams.”

Mix human memory with your data. It gives you strong context. These insights save you hours of digging through data.

How to Use This in Your Actual Work.

Once you spot a seasonal pattern, use it to guide your work.

Build simple baselines. Look at two to three years of data and note when dips and peaks usually happen. Add key factors like holidays or weather. Even one simple note like ‘Sales fall in Q3 and rise again in Q4’ helps a lot.

Add context to your dashboards. Never show one number alone. Include last month and the same month last year. A month to month dip looks scary until you see year to year growth.

Annotate your charts. Add small notes like “Holiday spike” or “School break dip.” This helps everyone understand the pattern without guessing.

Lead with context. When you present results, start by saying what is normal for that season. Then explain what is new or different. This keeps the focus on insight, not panic.

question: How do I explain both the benefits and drawbacks of a data-driven recommendation?
answer:
Explain the recommendation as a balanced story: start with the benefit, then name the drawback or risk, and end with what you want people to do. Isaac recommends asking, “What’s the good news?”, “What’s the bad news?”, and “What do I want people to do about it?”

Finally, tailor the explanation to the audience. The same metric can lead different people to different conclusions, so connect the benefit and drawback to the decision they need to make.

question: How can I measure something customer-related that isn’t directly visible?
answer:
Use a proxy metric, a measurable stand-in for the customer-related thing you cannot see directly. For customer happiness, Isaac suggests looking at repeat purchases, time on site, or support ticket volume. None measures happiness itself, but each gives clues.

Do not rely on just one proxy. Track several and look for the same pattern. For example, combine Repeat Purchase Rate, NPS, Average Order Value, Support Ticket Volume, and Time Between Purchases. When they point in the same direction, you can be more confident. When they conflict, investigate instead of assuming.

[chunk_id: the-measurement-problem-every-analyst#0] The Measurement Problem Every Analyst Faces (And How to Fix It) > The Measurement Problem Every Analyst Faces (And How to Fix It)
You want to know if your customers are happy.

But here’s the problem: you can’t just knock on someone’s door and ask, “Hey, on a scale of 1 to 10, how happy are you right now?”

Well, you could 😕, but good luck getting honest answers. People lie. People don’t know how they feel. And most importantly, you can’t do this for thousands of customers every single day.

So what do you do?

You use something called a Proxy Metric .

And if you learn this trick, you can solve a big data problem: how to measure things that feel impossible to measure.

---

[chunk_id: the-measurement-problem-every-analyst#2] The Measurement Problem Every Analyst Faces (And How to Fix It) > Let Me Show You an Example
Let’s say you run an online store.

You want happy customers. But you can’t read their minds.

So you pick a proxy: Repeat Purchase Rate .

If people keep coming back to buy from you, that’s a good sign they’re happy. If they buy once and never return, that’s a red flag.

Is this perfect? No. But it’s better than nothing.

Another easy example.

You sell furniture. You want to know if your furniture is good quality.

You can’t test every single chair and table. That would take forever.

So you pick a proxy: Return Rate .

If people keep sending your stuff back, your quality probably sucks. If almost no one returns anything, you’re doing something right.

Again, not perfect. But useful.

---

[chunk_id: the-measurement-problem-every-analyst#1] The Measurement Problem Every Analyst Faces (And How to Fix It) > Okay, But What Even Is a Proxy Metric?
A proxy metric is a stand-in. It’s something you can measure that stands for something you can’t measure directly.

Think of it like this:

You want to know if someone is rich. But you can’t see their bank account.

So instead, you look at their car. Their house. Their clothes. These things aren’t money, but they give you clues about money.

That’s a proxy.

In data, we do the same thing.

You want to measure: Customer Happiness

You can’t measure it directly because happiness lives in people’s heads.

So you find a proxy: Maybe it’s how often people come back to buy again (Repeat Purchase Rate). Maybe it’s how long they stay on your website (Time on Site). Maybe it’s how few complaints you get (Support Ticket Volume).

These aren’t happiness. But they leave clues about happiness.

---

[chunk_id: the-measurement-problem-every-analyst#4] The Measurement Problem Every Analyst Faces (And How to Fix It) > So How Do You Fix This?
Great analysts find one proxy metric.

Elite analysts use many proxy metrics together to get closer to the truth.

Here’s what that means.

Instead of using only one number, you track several proxies and look for patterns.

Let’s go back to the “Customer Happiness” example.

Triangulating Customer Happiness.

You want to know if customers are happy. So you track:

- Repeat Purchase Rate (Are they coming back?)

- Net Promoter Score (NPS) (Would they recommend you to a friend?)

- Average Order Value (Are they buying more over time?)

- Support Ticket Volume (Are they complaining?)

- Time Between Purchases (How often are they coming back?)

Now you’re not just looking at one shadow. You’re looking at five different shadows from five different angles.

If all five metrics point the same way, you can be pretty sure about what’s happening.

If Repeat Purchase Rate is up, NPS is up, Average Order Value is up, Support Tickets are down, and Time Between Purchases is shrinking, then yeah, your customers are probably happy.

But if Repeat Purchase Rate is up but NPS is down and Support Tickets are spiking, something weird is going on. Maybe people are buying because they have no other option, but they’re not actually happy about it.

That’s triangulation.

You’re using multiple proxies to get closer to the truth.

These charts may not look as flashy as a treemap, but they help the reader understand the data faster, which is the whole point of sharing data in the first place.

[chunk_id: the-problem-with-treemaps#2] The Problem With Treemaps > Small Categories Get Squeezed
Treemaps also have a problem with small categories.

When a few large values take up most of the space, the smaller values get squeezed into tiny boxes. Their labels may get cut off. Some labels may not show at all. The chart still looks full, but the details are no longer easy to read.

This happens a lot in business dashboards. One or two large groups take over the space, while the rest become tiny blocks. At that point, those small blocks only make sense if you hover over them with a mouse.

Tooltips are useful for this, but they should only support the chart, not carry the whole thing.

If someone has to hover over many boxes just to understand the basic message, the chart is not doing enough on its own. A good chart should give the main story without extra digging.

[chunk_id: the-problem-with-treemaps#0] The Problem With Treemaps > The Problem With Treemaps
Humans are good at comparing length when objects are lined up. That is why bar charts work so well.

If one bar is longer than another, we can usually spot the difference fast.

Treemaps do not work that way. They use area.

That means the reader has to compare one box with another. This sounds easy, but it is not. One box may look bigger because it is wider. Another may look bigger because it is taller. Two boxes can have almost the same area but very different shapes.

So the eye starts guessing.

If Category A is 18% and Category B is 16%, most people will not see that difference clearly in a treemap. They may need to hover, check labels, or look at the numbers. At that point, the chart is no longer helping enough.

A chart should not make basic comparison feel like a puzzle.

question: How can I tell whether my dashboard metrics actually measure what they claim?
answer: In “Stop Redesigning Broken Dashboards,” Isaac says to test the metric definition before judging the dashboard design. Ask what exactly counts, what is excluded, and whether everyone agrees on the logic. For example, define whether “active users” includes one login, specific actions, bots, test accounts, or internal users. Also check whether rules have changed and whether the report mixes things that should stay separate. If these answers are unclear, the metric may not mean the same thing to everyone, or may describe a problem that does not really exist.

[chunk_id: stop-redesigning-broken-dashboards#1] Stop Redesigning Broken Dashboards > Bad Metrics Do Not Announce Themselves
A broken metric does not always look broken. Most of them look completely normal on the surface.

The problem is in the definition, and you only notice the gaps when you look closely.

Take “active users.” It sounds simple. But what counts as active? Logging in once? Completing a specific action? Does the definition exclude bots, test accounts, or internal users?

If nobody has answered those questions clearly, the number means something different to every person looking at it.

Now take ‘churn rate.’ Most people think it means customers who canceled. But what about accounts that paused? Downgraded? Stopped paying but never fully closed?

If paused accounts are being counted as lost, churn looks worse than it actually is. The product gets blamed for a problem that may not exist in the way the data suggests.

These are not rare edge cases. They are the kinds of definition gaps that live inside common KPIs at real companies, often for years, with nobody raising a flag.

---

[chunk_id: stop-redesigning-broken-dashboards#4] Stop Redesigning Broken Dashboards > Design Last. Measure First.
The whole point of tracking data is to help people make better decisions. That only happens if the numbers measure exactly what they claim to measure.

Good design is meant to support good data, not replace it.

Before you start your next dashboard redesign, take a step back. Check your metrics. Make sure the logic behind the number is clear and that everyone agrees on it. Make sure the number is actually measuring what it claims to measure.

Once you trust the foundation, then you can start designing.

This means pausing to ask hard questions. They check if the rules have changed since the dashboard was first made. They check if the report is mixing things that should never be mixed.

Checking these details can feel very slow. It might even feel like you are creating problems instead of solving them. But these checks are the only way to keep the final report honest.

Without them, you just end up with a beautiful screen that tells a confident story about something that never really happened.

question: How can I tell whether strange data is an error or something meaningful?
answer:
Isaac says not to remove strange values just because they look inconvenient. First, study the pattern and ask what caused it. Check whether the unusual data is linked to a person, group, time, business rule or workaround. Missing values can also carry meaning, especially when they cluster in one group.

Then look outside the table. Talk to customers and the team, and check notes or daily records. These can reveal system problems, unusual users, business changes or other reasons the data looks strange. The key question is: “Why is this messy?”

[chunk_id: the-dirty-secret-every-senior-analyst#0] The Dirty Secret Every Senior Analyst Knows (But Won't Tell You) > The Dirty Secret Every Senior Analyst Knows (But Won't Tell You)
Data doesn't just appear. Humans create it.

And humans are weird, lazy, creative, and unpredictable.

That means every dataset you open is a mirror.

Not just of business processes, but of human behavior, pressure, habits, and workarounds. Clean it too fast, and you risk scrubbing away the most important clues.

This is the side of data work nobody talks about in tutorials.

The part that feels more like psychology than Python.

Let’s get into it.

In a sales dataset, if all the missing commission amounts belong to one manager, that's not a data quality issue. That's either a problem with their reporting system or they're hiding something.

If survey responses are missing for specific age groups, that's not random. That's telling you something about how those people interact with your survey method.

If timestamps cluster around certain hours, that's revealing when people actually use your product vs. when you think they do.

The pattern in what's NOT there is just as important as what IS there.

That person who bought 847 units of your product. Don't remove them. Find them. They might be running a business you didn't know existed.

Those users with session times of 14 hours. They're not errors. They're power users who left your app open, which tells you something important about your product's stickiness.

---

[chunk_id: the-gap-between-what-happened-and#3] The Gap Between What Happened And Why > What To Check After You See The Pattern
If your data cannot explain the reason, you need to look outside the table.

Talking to customers can tell you things no math ever will. When people stop buying your product, they rarely fill out a form to tell you why. But if you talk to ten of them, you will start to hear the same story over and over.

That kind of truth never shows up on a dashboard.

Your own team is another great place to look. If sales dropped last month, ask the sales team what was happening. Maybe they did not have enough workers. Maybe a big deal fell apart at the last minute, or everyone was stuck in training.

The data only shows the result. The team knows what happened behind the result.

Simple notes and daily records can also explain what the numbers miss. If a business changed its prices or switched delivery trucks during the time you are studying, that completely changes how you read the numbers.

---

[chunk_id: the-dirty-secret-every-senior-analyst#3] The Dirty Secret Every Senior Analyst Knows (But Won't Tell You) > People Work Around Broken Systems
When I see text like "see notes field" in a number column, I don't just convert it to null. I go find the notes field. Someone was trying to tell me something important that didn't fit in your neat little database schema.

That creative use of the "other" category is someone's telling you your options are incomplete.

The Questions Nobody Asks.

Instead of "How do I clean this data?" ask:

- "What was the person entering this data thinking?"

- "What business rule created this weird pattern?"

- "Who benefits if I clean this vs. keep it messy?"

- "What story does the mess tell that the clean data hides?"

- "Am I cleaning this because it's wrong, or because it's inconvenient?"

The most dangerous question in data analysis is "How do I make this cleaner?" The most valuable question is "Why is this messy?"

question: Which chart should I use to make my data easy to compare?

[chunk_id: the-bar-chart-mistake-most-analysts#2] The Bar Chart Mistake Most Analysts Make > Grouped Bars Make Comparing Easy

For example, let’s say you are comparing sales for three products across four regions. A grouped bar chart can work well because the reader can look at each region and compare the products beside each other.

question: How should I present disappointing results without making everyone defensive?
answer: Present the results calmly and start with what the data shows, not with an apology or dramatic warning. Add context to show you investigated the issue thoroughly, including trends, comparisons and other relevant analysis. Then explain the options and recommend the path you think is best, with evidence behind it. This keeps people focused on the problem rather than feeling blamed. For disappointing but non-critical updates, you can start with the bad news and end with something positive, especially when you are not asking for immediate action.

[chunk_id: nobody-wants-to-hear-bad-news-but#1] Nobody Wants to Hear Bad News, But Here's How to Tell Them Anyway > 1. Start with the Facts, Not Feelings
This is rule number one.

Don’t walk in saying “I have terrible news” or “This is really bad.”

Don’t apologize. Don’t sugarcoat it. Don’t make it dramatic. Just say what the data shows.

Bad way: “Guys, I’m really sorry, but the numbers this quarter are terrible. I know you’re not going to like this...”

Good way: “The data shows our customer retention dropped 15% last quarter.”

The first one makes everyone nervous before you even share the number. The second one is calm, clear, and factual.

When you stay neutral, people stay focused on the problem instead of their emotions.

---

[chunk_id: nobody-wants-to-hear-bad-news-but#3] Nobody Wants to Hear Bad News, But Here's How to Tell Them Anyway > 3. Show You Investigated Thoroughly
This step builds trust.

When you present bad news, people want to know: did you actually do the work? Or are you just showing me one chart and guessing?

Prove that you dug deep.

Show them you analyzed the data from multiple angles. That you looked at trends over time. That you compared it to benchmarks or competitors.

Example: “I looked at 500 customer exit surveys, analyzed purchasing patterns across 3 years, and compared our numbers against industry benchmarks.”

When people see you did the work, they trust your conclusions. And that makes them more willing to listen to your recommendations.

---

[chunk_id: nobody-wants-to-hear-bad-news-but#5] Nobody Wants to Hear Bad News, But Here's How to Tell Them Anyway > 5. Recommend a Path Forward
Don’t just list options and walk away. Take a position. Tell them which option you think is best and why.

This is where your expertise matters.

You’re the one who analyzed the data. You’re the one who understands the trends. You’re the one who knows what’s likely to work.

So say it.

Example: “I recommend Option B because our research shows customers value quality over price. 68% of exit surveys mentioned service issues, not cost. If we improve service, we can keep our pricing and still win customers back.”

When you make a clear recommendation backed by data, you make it easier for leaders to decide.

These five steps turn a scary presentation into a productive conversation. But there’s one more thing you need to understand...

Presenting bad news will never be fun. But it doesn’t have to be scary.

When you walk in with solid analysis, clear context, real solutions, and a recommended path forward, you’re not just delivering bad news.

You’re solving problems.

And that’s what good data analysts do.

So next time you have to present something nobody wants to hear, remember to start with the facts, add context, show your work, present options, and recommend a solution.

Do that, and you won’t just survive the meeting. You’ll walk out with people thanking you for catching the problem early.

When to use it:

- Sharing results that are disappointing but not critical

question: What should I compare a business result against to tell if it’s actually good?
answer:
Compare the result against the baseline that fits the business question. That might be last month, the same time last year, the company target, or an industry average.

Use targets to judge whether the business met its aim, past results to show progress, and the same period last year when seasonality affects the numbers. The key is to use the comparison that gives the clearest view of reality, not simply the easiest one.

[chunk_id: stop-comparing-everything-to-last#0] Stop Comparing Everything To Last Month > Stop Comparing Everything To Last Month

Maybe the company made $90,000 last month. Now $120,000 looks like an improvement. Maybe the goal was $150,000. Now that exact same number looks disappointing.

Or maybe the company made $140,000 at the same time last year. Now the business may actually be falling behind.

- Compared to last month/quarter/year: Shows trends

[chunk_id: eight-questions-every-dashboard-must#7] Eight Questions Every Dashboard Must Answer > Question 8: What Next?

- When?

- Where?

- How much?

- Compared to what?

- Why?
